text: A freshly provisioned GPU VM doesn't actually do anything with its GPU until three separate layers are installed and lined up: the NVIDIA driver, the CUDA toolkit, and the NVIDIA container toolkit. Each one has its own version number, each one does a genuinely different job, and getting GPU workloads running on Kubernetes next lesson depends on all three being correct here first.

The driver is a kernel module — it's what lets the operating system see the physical GPU at all. The CUDA toolkit sits above that in user space: the compiler and runtime libraries that frameworks like PyTorch actually link against. The container toolkit is the third piece, and it's the one people forget, because containers are isolated from the host by default, GPU included.

Installing the driver on a plain Ubuntu image is a straightforward apt install followed by a reboot. After that, nvidia-smi confirms it worked, printing the GPU model, the driver version, and a CUDA Version field in the corner — that number is the maximum CUDA release the driver supports, not necessarily what's installed, since the two are versioned independently by design.

The container toolkit closes the isolation gap: install the package, then run nvidia-ctk runtime configure to register the GPU runtime hook with Docker — skip that step and the toolkit sits there unused. The real proof it all works is docker run with --gpus all against a CUDA base image calling nvidia-smi from inside the container, and seeing the exact same GPU table the host reports.

That smoke test — driver on the host, CUDA toolkit present, container toolkit correctly wired into the runtime — is worth running against every new GPU node before trusting it with a real workload. Next lesson moves this up one level: making that same physical GPU visible to the Kubernetes scheduler as a resource pods can actually request, building directly on the device model from the Kubernetes course.
